title: Modifiers & Input
scopeHtml: Modifier chain semantics, custom modifiers (Modifier.Node vs composed), draw/layout modifiers, gestures and nested scroll, focus and keyboard, hit testing, semantics, and modifier performance.

questions.promptHtml: Why does the order of modifiers matter in Compose? What is the difference between Modifier.padding(16.dp).clickable { } and Modifier.clickable { }.padding(16.dp), and between background().padding() and padding().background()?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the most basic test of whether you understand that a modifier chain is an ordered wrapping of layout nodes, not a bag of properties like XML attributes.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A modifier chain is applied outside-in, left to right: each modifier wraps everything that comes after it. So clickable().padding() makes the padding part of the clickable area, while padding().clickable() shrinks the clickable area to the content inside the padding. Same for background: background().padding() paints behind the padding, padding().background() paints only the inner content. There is no margin in Compose, padding before a decoration acts like margin, padding after acts like padding.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Each modifier element sits in a linked chain. For layout modifiers, the parent constraints flow left to right (outer modifier first), and the measured size flows back right to left. Drawing and pointer input follow the same nesting: the modifier on the left wraps the ones on the right.

Modifier.clickable{}.padding(16.dp).background(Red)

[clickable area .................................]
 [padding 16dp ring                              ]
   [background Red + content]   <- only this is red

Modifier.padding(16.dp).clickable{}.background(Red)

[padding 16dp ring: no click, no paint]
   [clickable + red + content]

Official docs state the same example: with clickable before padding the entire area including padding responds to clicks; reversed, the padding ring does not react. Because order is explicit there is no margin concept; "margin" is just padding placed before background/clickable/border.

Other order-sensitive pairs: size before padding (padding eats into the fixed size) vs padding before size (padding adds outside); clip before background (background is clipped) vs after (not clipped); fillMaxWidth().padding() vs padding().fillMaxWidth() (both end up the same width here, but with size constraints they diverge); offset is applied where it sits and does not change measured size.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Whole 16dp ring is tappable and the ripple covers it
Text("A", Modifier.clickable { }.padding(16.dp))

// Ripple/tap area is only the text; ring is dead
Text("B", Modifier.padding(16.dp).clickable { })

// Rounded card: clip first so background and ripple are clipped
Box(Modifier.clip(RoundedCornerShape(12.dp)).background(Color.White).clickable { }.padding(16.dp))

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Debugging "my click area is too small" by changing sizes instead of reordering.
  • Putting clip after background/border and wondering why corners are square.
  • Assuming modifiers in the chain are commutative because they look like attributes.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is there no margin modifier? → Order makes it redundant: padding before a decoration is margin, after is padding.
  2. size(100.dp).padding(10.dp) vs padding(10.dp).size(100.dp)? → First: the box is 100 total, content is 80. Second: content is 100, total is 120 (subject to incoming max constraints).
  3. How do incoming constraints interact with size? → size is coerced into the parent's constraints; requiredSize ignores them and the parent centers the child.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "order matters, padding before is margin". Senior: explains chain nesting, constraints down / sizes up, and applies it to touch target, ripple bounds, clipping and Modifier.layout ordering, and can predict the result without running it.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A refactor swapped padding().clickable() for clickable().padding() (or the reverse) in a shared list-row component and either shrank every touch target or made empty gutters tappable and caused accidental navigation.

questions.promptHtml: What is a Modifier in Compose, and what are the conventions every reusable composable should follow regarding its modifier parameter?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks API design hygiene; sloppy modifier handling is the number-one review comment on design-system code.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Modifier is an immutable, ordered list of elements, each element adds one behavior: layout, draw, pointer input, semantics, focus. then concatenates two chains. By convention a composable takes modifier: Modifier = Modifier as its first optional parameter, applies it to the root-most emitted node only, and puts its own modifiers after the caller's (modifier.padding(...)) unless it needs to be outermost.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Modifier is an interface with a then(other) operator, Modifier (the companion) as the empty identity, and CombinedModifier as the linked pair. Modifier.Element is a single link. Because chains are values, they are cheap to compare and can be hoisted to constants: the docs recommend extracting chains used under frequent recomposition (animation, scroll state) to avoid re-allocating on every frame.

Conventions from the Compose API guidelines (and the modifiers doc):

  1. Every composable that emits UI accepts modifier: Modifier = Modifier, first optional parameter, after required ones.
  2. Apply it to the first (root) layout it emits, once. Do not apply to several children, and do not ignore it.
  3. Chain on the received modifier: modifier.fillMaxWidth(), not Modifier.fillMaxWidth().then(modifier) unless you deliberately need yours first.
  4. Never pass a caller's modifier down to deeper children as a "style bag".
  5. Scoped modifiers (weight, align, matchParentSize) only exist in RowScope/ColumnScope/BoxScope; extracted scoped modifiers must go to a direct child of the same scope.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun UserRow(user: User, onClick: () -> Unit, modifier: Modifier = Modifier) {
    Row(
        modifier = modifier          // caller's constraints/size first
            .fillMaxWidth()
            .clickable(onClick = onClick)
            .padding(16.dp),
        verticalAlignment = Alignment.CenterVertically
    ) { Text(user.name) }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Dropping the caller's modifier: Row(Modifier.fillMaxWidth()) ignores modifier.
  • Starting from Modifier inside a composable that returns a modifier: fun Modifier.foo() = Modifier.padding(..) silently discards the previous chain; always start from this.
  • Reusing an extracted Modifier.weight(1f) on a non-direct child where it does nothing.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why default to Modifier and not null? → The empty modifier is a no-op identity, no null checks.
  2. When should your own modifiers go before the caller's? → Rare: when you must guarantee behavior the caller cannot undo, e.g. a minimum touch target applied outermost.
  3. Is a modifier chain stable/skippable? → Chain elements are value-like; equal chains compare equal via element equals, which is why ModifierNodeElement needs correct equals.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "pass modifier as a parameter". Senior: states the placement/ordering contract, scope safety, hoisting for allocation, and this then rule for custom factories.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A design-system Card ignored its modifier; product teams could not set testTag or size, and tests had to find nodes by text.

questions.promptHtml: How does Modifier.pointerInput(key) work, what happens when a key changes, and what is the stale-capture bug with pointerInput(Unit)?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: pointerInput blocks are coroutines captured once; people write them like callbacks and ship bugs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: pointerInput launches a suspending block in a coroutine that lives as long as the modifier is attached. The block only restarts, cancelling the old coroutine, when a key changes. Any value captured by the lambda at launch time stays frozen, so pointerInput(Unit) { detectTapGestures { onClick() } } keeps calling the first onClick forever. Either pass the changing values as keys or read them via rememberUpdatedState.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Internally pointerInput creates a SuspendingPointerInputModifierNode. On attach (and on key change) it launches your block with a PointerInputScope. Inside, awaitPointerEventScope / awaitEachGesture suspend until the next event. The node delivers pointer events to the active await call. When keys change, the coroutine is cancelled and relaunched, so in-progress gesture state is lost (a drag in flight is cancelled).

recomposition #1: onClick = A  -> block launched, captures A
recomposition #2: onClick = B  -> key Unit unchanged -> block NOT restarted -> still calls A
with key onClick: #2 -> cancel block, relaunch capturing B (gesture in flight is dropped)

Two correct options:

  • Key by what the block reads: cheap, but restarts mid-gesture whenever it changes. Fine for rarely changing values; dangerous for values changing every frame (a restart per frame cancels drags).
  • val current by rememberUpdatedState(onClick) and key on Unit: no restarts, always the latest value.

With strong skipping (default from Kotlin 2.0.20 / Compose compiler 1.5.4+; verify for your version), lambdas with stable captures are remembered, so keying on a lambda restarts less often, but do not rely on that for correctness.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun Tappable(onTap: () -> Unit, modifier: Modifier = Modifier) {
    val currentOnTap by rememberUpdatedState(onTap)
    Box(modifier.pointerInput(Unit) {
        detectTapGestures { currentOnTap() } // always latest, never restarts
    })
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• pointerInput(Unit) reading a var from the surrounding scope and acting on a stale snapshot (selection mode flag, list index).
  • Keying on a value that changes during the gesture, so the drag is cancelled after the first move.
  • Doing heavy setup inside the block on each restart.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is the lambda body executed every recomposition? → No, only on attach and key change.
  2. Does remember inside pointerInput work? → No; the block is not composable. Hoist state outside.
  3. Why prefer Modifier.clickable where possible? → It handles keys/updated lambdas internally and adds semantics, focus, indication.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE knows keys exist. Senior explains coroutine lifecycle, mid-gesture cancellation on restart, and chooses rememberUpdatedState vs key per update frequency.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: "Delete" in a swipe row removed the wrong item after a list reorder because the pointerInput block captured the original index.

questions.promptHtml: Why can't you put detectTapGestures and detectDragGestures in the same pointerInput block, and when should you use clickable versus pointerInput { detectTapGestures }?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you know detectors are suspending loops and the abstraction ladder (component, gesture modifier, raw pointerInput).

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Detectors like detectTapGestures are suspend functions that run an event loop until the coroutine is cancelled, so a second detector after it is never reached. Use one pointerInput per detector. Prefer clickable/combinedClickable for normal clicks because they add semantics, keyboard and focus support, hover and indication; drop to pointerInput only when you need tap position, no indication (a scrim), or custom gestures.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The official docs say: gesture modifiers on top of components give you accessibility and tested behavior, pointerInput gives raw control. Button announces as button in TalkBack; a bare clickable does not unless you set role.

Two stacked pointerInput modifiers each get their own coroutine and both see events (the same pointer can feed both because both are in the same hit chain; the earlier in the chain is outer). Because tap and drag both consume, they negotiate through consumption: the tap detector gives up when the pointer moves beyond touch slop and the drag detector claims the movement.

Custom pieces: awaitEachGesture restarts the block after all pointers lift (preferred to while(true)). Low-level helpers: awaitFirstDown, waitForUpOrCancellation, awaitTouchSlopOrCancellation, awaitLongPressOrCancellation, drag. detectDragGesturesAfterLongPress covers "long press then drag" (reorder handles).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Box(
    Modifier
        .size(100.dp)
        .pointerInput(Unit) { detectTapGestures(onDoubleTap = { zoomIn(it) }) }
        .pointerInput(Unit) {
            detectDragGestures { change, delta ->
                change.consume()
                pan += delta
            }
        }
)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Two detectors in one block: the second silently never runs.
  • Using raw pointerInput for a button and shipping an inaccessible control (no role, no click action, no focus).
  • Forgetting change.consume() inside drag callbacks.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you get the tap position with clickable? → You can't; use detectTapGestures.
  2. How do you add double tap to a clickable? → combinedClickable(onDoubleClick=...); note it delays single click by the double-tap timeout.
  3. How would you build "tap, double tap, long press, drag" on one element? → Separate pointerInput blocks, or write one awaitEachGesture state machine to control arbitration precisely.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: knows detectTapGestures. Senior: explains why detectors block, chooses abstraction level for a11y, and understands arbitration by consumption.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "tap to dismiss scrim" built with clickable showed a ripple over the whole screen and was reachable by keyboard focus; it was rebuilt with pointerInput plus explicit semantics.

questions.promptHtml: Explain how pointer events propagate in Compose: hit testing, the Initial/Main/Final passes, and what consume() does and does not do.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Gesture conflicts (swipe in scroll, button in clickable row) are solved only if you know who sees events first and what consumption means.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: On the first down, Compose hit-tests the tree and builds a chain of nodes that have pointer input and contain the touch; that same chain receives all later events for that pointer even outside bounds. Each event travels the chain in three passes: Initial (parent to child, so parents can intercept), Main (child to parent, where gestures normally consume), Final (parent to child, so parents learn what children consumed). consume() only marks the change as consumed; it does not stop delivery, so handlers must check isConsumed and opt out.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Facts from the docs: only the topmost sibling (by z-index) is hit unless a custom PointerInputModifierNode sets sharePointerInputWithSiblings. Hover events are the exception and go to whichever node is currently hovered.

Initial  : Root -> ... -> Leaf     (tooltip intercepts long press here)
Main     : Leaf -> ... -> Root     (default; Button consumes, row ignores)
Final    : Root -> ... -> Leaf     (ripple cancels when parent scroll consumed)

Because Main goes leaf-first, the innermost clickable wins over an outer clickable. A scrollable parent does not consume the down, it waits for movement beyond touch slop and then consumes the drag; children then see the change as consumed in Final and cancel (that is how a pressed ripple disappears when you start scrolling).

PointerInputChange has consume(), isConsumed, and position/previous-position data. Consumption is cooperative: nothing prevents a handler from ignoring isConsumed. Standard detectors check it.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Modifier.pointerInput(Unit) {
    awaitEachGesture {
        val down = awaitFirstDown(pass = PointerEventPass.Initial) // parent-first peek
        // intercept long presses before children see them
        val ev = awaitPointerEvent(PointerEventPass.Initial)
        if (ev.changes.none { it.isConsumed }) { /* handle */ }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Believing consume() blocks siblings or parents from receiving the event.
  • Handling in the wrong pass and losing to a child.
  • Expecting events to stop arriving when the finger leaves bounds mid-gesture.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Two overlapping buttons in a Box, which gets the tap? → Only the one on top (higher z-order); the other gets nothing.
  2. How do you intercept child gestures? → Handle in the Initial pass and consume there.
  3. How do hover events differ? → They are not chained; delivered to whichever node is under the pointer.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "child handles first". Senior: names passes, uses Initial for interception, explains touch slop arbitration and why consumption is advisory.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A bottom sheet inside a vertically scrolling screen stole drags because both consumed in Main; moving arbitration to nested scroll fixed it.

questions.contextHtml:
A grocery app has a multi-select list. Long-press enters selection mode and then taps toggle selection. QA reports: after selecting item 3, tapping other items still navigates to the detail screen (as if selection mode were off) about 100% of the time, but only on the first screen visit; after rotating the device it works. No crash, no log. The code:

@Composable
fun ProductRow(p: Product, selecting: Boolean, onOpen: (Product) -> Unit, onToggle: (Product) -> Unit) {
    Text(
        p.name,
        Modifier.fillMaxWidth().pointerInput(Unit) {
            detectTapGestures(
                onLongPress = { onToggle(p) },
                onTap = { if (selecting) onToggle(p) else onOpen(p) }
            )
        }.padding(16.dp)
    )
}
questions.promptHtml: Find the bug, explain why rotation hides it, and fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "State isn't updating, use a ViewModel/remember." It treats it as a state problem and never identifies that the gesture block is not re-executed.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is selecting a State hoisted above the row (yes in this case, otherwise the symptom would be different)? Does the row's key stay stable across selection (list reuse)? Which Compose version and is strong skipping on (affects whether lambdas change identity)? Does it repro in rows that scrolled in after selection started (it does not, those capture the new value)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add selecting (and p) as keys: pointerInput(selecting, p).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) stale capture in pointerInput(Unit); (b) the parent is not recomposing with the new selecting (disproved: new rows work); (c) lazy item keys wrong (disproved by rotation behavior); (d) click consumed by a child (no child).
  4. How I'd verify: Log inside onTap to see selecting; Layout Inspector shows the row recomposed with selecting=true while the handler still sees false; adding a key fixes it.
  5. Root cause: The block is launched once with the first-composition captures (selecting=false). Recomposition creates new lambda instances but the running coroutine keeps using the old closure. Rotation recreates composition so the block relaunches with current values; rows scrolled in later capture new values.
  6. Fix: Short-term keys. Better: val sel by rememberUpdatedState(selecting) and read inside callbacks, so long-press-drag gestures in flight are not cancelled by key changes. Long-term: prefer combinedClickable(onClick, onLongClick), which handles updated lambdas internally and adds semantics.
  7. Prevention: Lint/review rule: pointerInput(Unit) that references any non-constant value is a smell; add a UI test that toggles mode then taps.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not key on p if the gesture is long (restart cancels drag). I would not move to mutableStateOf inside the pointerInput block.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if I key on selecting and the user is mid-long-press when it flips? → The coroutine restarts and the gesture is dropped; use rememberUpdatedState.
  • Does strong skipping fix it? → No; it affects lambda identity, not captured closure inside a running coroutine.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite incident: a "bulk archive" feature shipped with this bug and users archived the wrong mail after sort order changed because the captured item index was stale; the fix was a one-line rememberUpdatedState, the postmortem added a lint check.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames state holder; cannot explain why rotation changes behavior.
  • Hire: identifies stale capture and adds keys.
  • Strong hire: contrasts keys vs rememberUpdatedState, mentions mid-gesture cancellation and combinedClickable, adds a regression test.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between drawBehind, drawWithContent, and graphicsLayer, and why does reading state inside their lambdas avoid recomposition?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The core Compose performance idea (phase-scoped state reads) shows up here in its most practical form.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: drawBehind draws under the content, drawWithContent lets me draw before/after and decide when to call drawContent(), and graphicsLayer applies transformations (alpha, scale, rotation, translation, clip) on a GPU-backed layer without re-layout. All of their lambdas run in the draw phase (or layer-update phase), and snapshot state read inside them invalidates only that phase, not composition. So animating a color or translation through the lambda version skips recomposition and often layout.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Compose has three phases: composition, layout, draw. A state read registers with the scope that is active when it is read. Reading scrollOffset in composition (Modifier.offset(x = offset.dp)) re-runs composition and layout each change. Reading it in Modifier.offset { IntOffset(offset, 0) } (layout phase) skips composition. Reading it in Modifier.graphicsLayer { translationX = offset } or drawBehind { } skips composition and layout and only re-records the draw/layer. This is called deferring reads; the official performance docs list it as a core practice.

Modifier Phase Typical use
drawBehind {} draw background shapes, underline, badges
drawWithContent {} draw overlay, mask, conditional content
graphicsLayer {} lambda layer/draw translation, scale, rotation, alpha animated
offset {} (lambda) layout (placement) position that changes often

graphicsLayer(alpha = x) with a non-lambda argument reads x in composition; use the lambda form for animated values. Modifier.clip is implemented with graphicsLayer (per the custom modifier docs).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun Badge(progress: State<Float>) {
    Box(
        Modifier
            .size(48.dp)
            .graphicsLayer { alpha = progress.value }      // draw-phase read
            .drawBehind { drawCircle(Color.Red, radius = size.minDimension / 2 * progress.value) }
    )
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Passing animatedFloat.value as a plain argument (alpha = a.value) which recomposes every frame.
  • Creating offscreen layers needlessly (graphicsLayer with alpha < 1 or CompositingStrategy.Offscreen) on large views.
  • Drawing with drawBehind something that should be a real composable (not accessible).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. offset(x.dp) vs offset { }? → The first reads in composition, the second in layout placement; use the lambda for frequently changing values.
  2. Does graphicsLayer change hit testing? → Pointer input honors layer transforms (translation/scale) in the chain; test it.
  3. When does graphicsLayer cost memory? → Layers with Offscreen strategy or render effects allocate a buffer.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: draw APIs. Senior: ties each lambda to its phase and shows the recomposition counter staying at 0 in Layout Inspector.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A progress ring recomposed its entire card 60 times per second; moving the animated value into drawBehind/graphicsLayer lambdas dropped recompositions to zero.

questions.promptHtml: How does Compose decide whether a touch hits a composable, and how do you guarantee a 48dp minimum touch target for a small icon?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Touch target bugs are the most common accessibility and usability finding, and they come directly from modifier order and bounds.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Hit testing uses the layout bounds of the node that carries the pointer-input modifier, so the touchable area is the size at the point in the chain where clickable sits. A 24dp icon with clickable is 24dp. Material components (IconButton, Button, Checkbox) enforce at least 48dp via the minimum interactive component size; for custom elements I put clickable first and the padding or size(48.dp) after it, or wrap with minimumInteractiveComponentSize().

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A pointer-input modifier is a node in the chain; its bounds are the layout bounds of everything to its right. Modifiers to its left (outer) are not part of its hit area. So:

Icon(24dp).clickable{}.padding(12.dp)  -> hit area: 48dp (clickable wraps the padding)
Icon(24dp).padding(12.dp).clickable{}  -> hit area: 24dp

Material 3 enforces the minimum size through minimumInteractiveComponentSize() using LocalMinimumInteractiveComponentSize (older names: minimumTouchTargetSize, LocalMinimumTouchTargetEnforcement; verify the name in your Material version). It grows the layout footprint to 48dp but keeps drawing small. Hit slop can extend beyond parent bounds only if a parent does not clip and the node is within the hit chain; a parent whose bounds do not contain the touch will not be hit-tested into children (hit testing walks down from the root through bounds), which is why enlarged touch areas via offset outside the parent get lost.

Also: Modifier.pointerInput hit areas change with graphicsLayer transforms; and transparent regions still count (bounds, not pixels).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Icon(
    Icons.Default.Close, contentDescription = "Close",
    modifier = Modifier
        .clickable(role = Role.Button, onClick = onClose)
        .padding(12.dp)       // after clickable -> inside the hit area
        .size(24.dp)
)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• padding before clickable for "spacing" and unknowingly shrinking the target.
  • Using Modifier.size(24.dp).clickable on dense toolbars.
  • Expanding a target with offset and finding taps outside the parent bounds are dropped.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does 48dp need to be visible? → No, it is the interactive footprint; visuals can be smaller.
  2. Two adjacent 48dp targets overlap after expansion? → Hit goes to the topmost; keep adjacency or add spacing.
  3. How do tests verify it? → Accessibility Scanner flags it; Compose tests can assert size with assertTouchHeightIsEqualTo / assertTouchWidthIsEqualTo.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "use IconButton". Senior: explains bounds-based hit testing, where minimum size comes from, why parent bounds clip expanded targets, and verifies with tests.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Accessibility review rejected a redesigned toolbar because icons were 24dp touch targets after a refactor reordered padding and clickable.

questions.contextHtml:
A messaging app (4M DAU) ships a toolbar refresh. Next day support tickets spike: "buttons don't respond", and analytics show the tap-through rate on the search icon dropped from 6.2% to 4.1% of sessions with no UI change in visibility. Crash rate unchanged. The refresh replaced IconButton with a shared helper:

fun Modifier.iconTap(onClick: () -> Unit) =
    this.padding(10.dp).clickable(onClick = onClick).size(24.dp)

Devices mostly 2.75-3x density phones. No errors in logcat.
questions.promptHtml: How do you diagnose and fix this, and how do you stop it recurring?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Probably a slow backend or a lost listener", rolling back the whole release, or increasing icon size visually without understanding hit area; no explanation of order.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Did the drop correlate with the release version? Which icons (all that use the helper)? Is it worse on larger-finger/accessibility users or font/display scaling? Did anything change in parent clipping or z-order? Do replays show repeated taps near the icon (rage taps)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix the helper by reordering to clickable first with padding after, or ship via remote-config-gated fix; rollback only if the fix is not ready same day.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) touch target shrank because padding precedes clickable (24dp hit area); (b) overlapping sibling intercepts; (c) parent clipping; (d) disabled state logic; (e) analytics event regression.
  4. How I'd verify: Layout Inspector (bounds overlay) shows 24dp bounds for the clickable node; a Compose test assertTouchWidthIsEqualTo(48.dp) fails; Accessibility Scanner flags "touch target size"; adb shell input tap at 12dp from the center fails.
  5. Root cause: The pointer-input node sits to the right of padding, so hit bounds are 24dp, not 48dp. A 24dp target on ~3x density is 72px; thumb contact area exceeds it, so a significant share of taps land in the dead ring.
  6. Fix: this.clickable(role = Role.Button, onClick = onClick).padding(12.dp).size(24.dp) or minimumInteractiveComponentSize(); better, return to IconButton which also gives ripple bounds and semantics.
  7. Prevention: Screenshot/semantics tests asserting touch size for every shared icon component; lint or review checklist for custom clickable helpers; Accessibility Scanner in CI on key screens.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not just bump size visually (design change) or add offset hacks; I would not wait for next train if analytics show a conversion drop.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if design requires the icons packed 32dp apart? → Keep 48dp targets overlapping only in padding, accept it, or enforce spacing; Material guidance wants ~8dp between targets.
  • Why did rotation not matter? → Hit bounds are density-based; only dp size matters.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite case where a "tiny helper" in a shared module silently shrank targets across 40 screens; the lasting fix was a golden test per shared component that asserts touch bounds.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: guesses at backend or rollback; no tool use.
  • Hire: spots the modifier order and fixes it.
  • Strong hire: quantifies target size/density, adds automated touch-size tests and shared-component guardrails.

questions.promptHtml: Why is Modifier.composed {} discouraged, how does Modifier.Node work, and how do you write a custom modifier correctly?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A senior must write reusable modifiers without hidden per-recomposition and per-node composition cost.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: composed {} runs a composable factory for every node the modifier is applied to, making it a mini-composition per use, it is never skipped, allocates remembers per node, and cannot be hoisted. Modifier.Node splits it into a stateless ModifierNodeElement (data-like, with equals) created every recomposition and a long-lived stateful Modifier.Node that is created once and updated in place when equals is false. The docs now recommend Node for anything beyond chaining existing modifiers.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Three tiers of custom modifier:

  1. Chain existing modifiers in an extension function (cheapest, preferred).
  2. Composable modifier factory (@Composable fun Modifier.x(): Modifier), allowed when you need remember/animations/CompositionLocals, with caveats from the docs: never skipped (it returns a value), only callable inside composition, and CompositionLocals are resolved at the call site where the modifier is created, not where it is applied.
  3. ModifierNodeElement + Modifier.Node: create() once, update(node) when equals differs, auto-invalidation of the relevant phase, implements node interfaces: DrawModifierNode, LayoutModifierNode, PointerInputModifierNode, SemanticsModifierNode, CompositionLocalConsumerModifierNode, ObserverModifierNode, DelegatingNode, etc. Nodes have coroutineScope, onAttach, onDetach, onReset.
recomposition -> new Element (cheap, stateless, equals?)
        equal   -> nothing
        differs -> element.update(existingNode)  -> invalidate draw/layout automatically

Key rules: element must implement correct equals/hashCode (data class), update must mutate the existing node rather than allocate, nodes can be reused (onReset). You can set shouldAutoInvalidate = false and call invalidateDraw() / invalidateMeasurement() yourself to avoid invalidating layout when only color changes. Composition locals are read in a node via currentValueOf(LocalX) in a snapshot-observed scope (draw, measure, semantics) or observeReads in an ObserverModifierNode.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun Modifier.dot(color: Color) = this then DotElement(color)

private data class DotElement(val color: Color) : ModifierNodeElement<DotNode>() {
    override fun create() = DotNode(color)
    override fun update(node: DotNode) { node.color = color }
}

private class DotNode(var color: Color) : Modifier.Node(), DrawModifierNode {
    override fun ContentDrawScope.draw() { drawCircle(color); drawContent() }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting this then and dropping the existing chain.
  • Using a lambda in the element without stable equality, so update fires every recomposition (lambdas compare by instance unless remembered).
  • Retaining stale state in a reused node: reset in onReset/onAttach.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why can't composed be skipped? → It is a composable returning a value; such functions are not skippable.
  2. How do you share state across modifiers? → DelegatingNode delegating to child nodes (the docs show a clickable node sharing interaction data).
  3. What if the element is an object/no params? → Use data object (no update work) as in the docs' fixed padding example.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "use composed". Senior: knows the cost model, writes Nodes, controls invalidation, resolves CompositionLocals at the use site correctly.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A composed shimmer applied to 200 list rows showed up as the top composition cost; the Node version removed per-row composition work.

questions.contextHtml:
Feed screen, LazyColumn with items showing a skeleton shimmer while images load. Shimmer is implemented as:

fun Modifier.shimmer(visible: Boolean): Modifier = composed {
    val t = rememberInfiniteTransition(label = "s")
    val x by t.animateFloat(0f, 1000f, infiniteRepeatable(tween(1200)), label = "x")
    if (!visible) this else drawWithContent {
        drawContent(); drawRect(brush = Brush.linearGradient(listOf(Color.LightGray, Color.White, Color.LightGray), start = Offset(x, 0f), end = Offset(x + 400f, 0f)))
    }
}

Up to 12 items on screen with shimmer. Mid-range device (Pixel 6a class): p95 frame time during first scroll 19 ms at 60 Hz (budget 16.6 ms), 14% janky frames; Layout Inspector shows every shimmering item recomposing every frame.
questions.promptHtml: Why is this slow and how do you redesign it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Reduce the animation or use fewer items." Or wraps in remember without understanding that x is read in composition.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is jank only during scroll or also idle? Do all shimmering items need independent phases (design says no)? Release build and baseline profile? Do I have a macrobenchmark scroll baseline?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ship a flag that disables shimmer under low-end device class or when scrolling fast; use static placeholders.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) x read in composition via by delegate inside composed, so each item recomposes per frame; (b) 12 independent infinite transitions; (c) composed overhead per node per recomposition; (d) gradient shader reallocation each draw; (e) image decode (red herring).
  4. How I'd verify: Layout Inspector recomposition counters climb at 60/s per item; Perfetto trace shows composition slices every frame; compose compiler report; Macrobenchmark FrameTimingMetric before/after.
  5. Root cause: The animated value is a State read inside the composed factory body (composition phase) rather than inside the draw lambda, so every frame invalidates composition of the host composable; multiplied by 12 items, with a composed factory that can't be skipped.
  6. Fix: Short-term: hoist one shared Float State (single transition) and read it inside drawWithContent via a State parameter, not by delegate. Long-term: a Modifier.Node implementing DrawModifierNode that reads a shared State<Float>/Animatable in draw() so only draw is invalidated; cache the Brush and update its offset with translate/shader local matrix instead of reallocating.
  7. Prevention: Macrobenchmark scroll test in CI with a regression threshold; review rule: animated values are read in lambdas only; compose recomposition-count assertions in debug builds.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not remove shimmer for everyone before measuring; I would not keep per-item transitions, a shared clock keeps items in sync which designers prefer.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if shimmer must start at the same visual time for all items? → Shared clock does that by definition.
  • Can Modifier.Node use a CompositionLocal for the shared clock? → Yes, CompositionLocalConsumerModifierNode.currentValueOf inside draw.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team found 25% of their frame budget in a "decorative" modifier; the fix was a 40-line Node and a benchmark that guarded it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tunes duration or removes items.
  • Hire: moves read to draw phase and shares one transition.
  • Strong hire: builds a Node, measures with Macrobenchmark, and adds CI guard.

questions.promptHtml: How does nested scrolling work in Compose, and how do you use NestedScrollConnection to build a collapsing header?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Coordinating scrollable and non-scrollable parents (collapsing toolbars, pull to refresh, bottom sheets) is a staple senior UI task.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Scrollable children (LazyColumn, verticalScroll, scrollable) dispatch scroll deltas up the nested-scroll chain before and after consuming them themselves. An ancestor with Modifier.nestedScroll(connection) can intercept in onPreScroll (before the child), react to leftovers in onPostScroll (after), and the same for flings with onPreFling/onPostFling. For a collapsing header I consume part of the delta in onPreScroll to shrink the header, return what I consumed, and the list gets the rest.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Order for a drag on a child scrollable: pre-scroll to ancestors (outermost-first or as the parent chain order), child consumes, post-scroll to ancestors with leftover. Each callback returns the amount consumed (Offset/Velocity). Flings repeat: onPreFling(available), child fling, onPostFling(consumed, available) (suspend functions). NestedScrollSource identifies user input vs fling/animation side effects (names changed across versions: Drag/Fling vs UserInput/SideEffect; verify in your version).

finger -> LazyColumn.dispatchScroll(delta)
          1) parent.onPreScroll(delta)      -> returns consumed c1
          2) child scrolls (delta - c1)     -> consumed c2
          3) parent.onPostScroll(c2, delta - c1 - c2)

Scroll cooperation is automatic only when parent has the nestedScroll modifier or is a scrollable container; a plain Modifier.offset parent knows nothing. Nested scrolling in the same direction with infinite constraints (a LazyColumn inside verticalScroll) is not supported and throws "Vertically scrollable component was measured with an infinity maximum height constraints".

Material's TopAppBarScrollBehavior is a ready-made nested-scroll implementation (exit-until-collapsed, enter-always, pinned).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class HeaderConnection(private val maxPx: Float) : NestedScrollConnection {
    var offset by mutableFloatStateOf(0f)   // 0..-maxPx, read in layout/draw lambdas
    override fun onPreScroll(available: Offset, source: NestedScrollSource): Offset {
        val next = (offset + available.y).coerceIn(-maxPx, 0f)
        val consumed = next - offset
        offset = next
        return Offset(0f, consumed)       // consume only what we used
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Returning available (consuming everything) so the list never scrolls.
  • Reading offset in composition, recomposing on every drag frame.
  • Ignoring fling: header stops mid-state and feels sticky; handle onPreFling / snap.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When to use onPostScroll? → Pull to refresh at the top: child cannot scroll further, leftover overscroll arrives post.
  2. onPreScroll vs onPostScroll for collapsing? → Collapse-first: Pre; list-first then collapse: Post.
  3. How does it interact with Views? → NestedScrollInteropConnection bridges with Views inside Compose (interop chunk covers it).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: knows TopAppBar behaviors. Senior: writes the connection, handles fling/snap, defers reads to layout/graphicsLayer lambdas, and reasons about scroll sources.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A custom collapsing header read its offset in composition and dropped frames on every scroll until reads moved into graphicsLayer {}.

questions.contextHtml: Product wants a profile screen: a 280dp cover photo header that collapses to a 56dp toolbar as the user scrolls a LazyColumn of 500+ posts; the header contains a parallax image (0.5x speed), a title that fades/scales, and a "Follow" button that must stay tappable at all times. Targeting low-end Android 8+ devices, 120 Hz devices exist. A prototype using offset(y = scrollState.firstVisibleItemScrollOffset.dp) recomposes the whole screen each frame and the Follow button taps sometimes fail during collapse.
questions.promptHtml: Design this: what mechanism do you choose, where are state reads, and how do you handle fling and the tap bug?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use CoordinatorLayout via AndroidView", or a header as the first LazyColumn item so it scrolls away (not pinned), or reading offset in composition.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Collapse-first or list-first? Should header re-expand only at list top (exit-until-collapsed) or on any scroll up? Snap behavior required? Accessibility requirements for the button? Same design for tablets?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Disable parallax on low-end devices and keep a simple pinned toolbar.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (for the prototype's problems): (a) offset read in composition; (b) offset(Dp) moves visually but touch bounds updated one frame late or the header drawn outside parent bounds; (c) header is a sibling beneath the list in z-order so the list steals taps.
  4. How I'd verify: Layout Inspector recomposition counts; Perfetto frames; hit-test debugging by logging bounds; semantics tree bounds for the button.
  5. Root cause: Scroll position read as a composition input, plus header in the wrong z-order or clipped by a parent, so hit testing excluded the moving button area.
  6. Fix: A NestedScrollConnection (or Material TopAppBarScrollBehavior) owning a single headerOffset State clamped to [-224dp, 0]. onPreScroll consumes while collapsing on scroll-up-of-content, optionally onPostScroll re-expansion at list top. The header composable reads progress inside graphicsLayer {} (parallax translation, alpha, scale) and offset {} (layout), so composition runs zero times during the gesture. Place the list with contentPadding equal to header height, header drawn above in a Box with higher z-index (zIndex) so the Follow button gets taps; because layout bounds follow the offset {} placement, hit testing matches. Add onPreFling snapping to collapsed/expanded via Animatable.
  7. Prevention: Macrobenchmark scroll test at 120 Hz device, a test asserting the button is displayed and clickable at collapsed and expanded states, performTouchInput { swipeUp() } in tests.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use AndroidView + CoordinatorLayout (interop cost, two systems); I would not make header a LazyColumn item if it must be pinned; I would not animate with animateDpAsState on scroll (adds lag).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What about accessibility focus order? → Header first in semantics order, collapsed state exposes a concise title; use semantics { heading() }.
  • What if a nested LazyRow of stories sits in the header? → Different axis nests fine; same-axis would require custom connection.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team replaced a state-driven parallax with draw-phase reads and cut frame time on low-end devices by roughly a third, measured with a benchmark rather than eyeballed.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: composition-level offsets, no touch plan.
  • Hire: nested scroll connection and lambda reads.
  • Strong hire: addresses fling/snap, z-order/hit-testing, accessibility and benchmarking.

questions.promptHtml: Compare scrollable, draggable, anchoredDraggable, draggable2D and transformable. How do you choose, and what do they not do for you?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Picking the right gesture primitive avoids hand-rolled pointerInput code with missing fling, slop and accessibility behavior.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: scrollable and draggable only detect gestures and report deltas; I must hold state and move the content. scrollable participates in nested scroll and fling; draggable is single-axis raw drag. anchoredDraggable snaps between discrete anchors with state, fling and animation, ideal for bottom sheets and swipe-to-reveal. draggable2D moves in both axes without fling. transformable handles multi-touch pan/zoom/rotate. For ready cases (SwipeToDismissBox, sheets, Slider) use the component.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
From the official docs: Choose Material components first; draggable when you only need raw deltas (custom slider); draggable2D for continuous XY (FAB the user can drag, map pan) with no fling (movement stops when the finger lifts); anchoredDraggable for discrete positions with DraggableAnchors, AnchoredDraggableState (saved with rememberSaveable and its Saver), offset read via state.requireOffset(). Anchors depend on measured size, so update them in a layout or onSizeChanged and call updateAnchors.

API Reports Moves content? Fling Nested scroll
scrollable scroll delta no yes yes
draggable drag delta no callback only no
anchoredDraggable offset in anchors via offset animates to anchor partial (via connection)
draggable2D 2D delta no no no
transformable pan/zoom/rotation no no no

Each reports deltas in pixels in the pointer direction (for scrollable the sign is the raw direction; scrollableArea inverts it so content follows the finger).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
var offsetX by remember { mutableFloatStateOf(0f) }
Text("Drag", Modifier
    .offset { IntOffset(offsetX.roundToInt(), 0) }   // read in layout, not composition
    .draggable(Orientation.Horizontal, state = rememberDraggableState { offsetX += it }))

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Expecting draggable to move the node: it only reports.
  • Reading the offset in composition for an anchored component.
  • Using pointerInput for dragging and losing touch slop, velocity tracking and accessibility semantics.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How is fling modeled for draggable? → onDragStopped(velocity) gives velocity; you animate yourself.
  2. Why rememberSaveable for anchored state? → Survive rotation; docs recommend with AnchoredDraggableState.Saver.
  3. draggable vs detectDragGestures? → The former is a ready modifier with interaction source, enabled flag, and semantic-friendly state; the latter is raw but allows 2D and custom start.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: lists modifiers. Senior: maps each to use cases, state ownership, fling, nested scroll interplay and accessibility alternatives (keyboard/semantic actions).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A hand-rolled swipe-to-reveal built on pointerInput had no fling and broke inside a LazyColumn; moving to anchoredDraggable fixed both.

questions.contextHtml:
A task app has a LazyColumn of rows; each row has a drag handle for reordering. QA: "dragging the handle also scrolls the list, rows jump around, and 1 in 5 drags drops the item in the wrong place." 8% of users who reorder abandon the screen. Code:

@Composable
fun Handle(onDrag: (Float) -> Unit, onEnd: () -> Unit) {
    Icon(
        Icons.Default.DragHandle, contentDescription = null,
        modifier = Modifier.pointerInput(Unit) {
            detectVerticalDragGestures(
                onVerticalDrag = { _, dy -> onDrag(dy) },
                onDragEnd = { onEnd() }
            )
        }
    )
}
questions.promptHtml: Why does the list scroll while the handle is dragged and why are drops inconsistent? Fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Disable scrolling in the LazyColumn with a flag" and no understanding of consumption; or "wrap in a Box" cargo-culting.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is reorder driven by live state in the ViewModel? Items keyed? Does it happen with a mouse/stylus as well? Which Compose version (detector signatures changed)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Turn reorder behind a flag and offer move up/down buttons.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) drag changes never consumed (the PointerInputChange is ignored), so the list's scrollable also drags; (b) pointerInput(Unit) captures stale onDrag (index changes as items reorder); (c) unkeyed items so state jumps; (d) handle tap area tiny.
  4. How I'd verify: Log change.isConsumed in the parent via a debug pointerInput in the Initial pass; scroll position logging; test with performTouchInput { swipeDown }; check list keys.
  5. Root cause: The onVerticalDrag callback receives the change; it is the app's job to consume it. Without change.consume() (ignoring the first parameter _), the same movement is also handled by the parent's scrollable in the Main pass, so the list scrolls. The stale onDrag closure explains inconsistent drops because the index reflects the first composition.
  6. Fix: Consume, use detectDragGesturesAfterLongPress or a handle-only vertical detector, and use rememberUpdatedState:
val currentDrag by rememberUpdatedState(onDrag)
val currentEnd by rememberUpdatedState(onEnd)
Modifier.pointerInput(Unit) {
    detectVerticalDragGestures(
        onVerticalDrag = { change, dy -> change.consume(); currentDrag(dy) },
        onDragEnd = { currentEnd() }, onDragCancel = { currentEnd() })
}

Add stable key to items. Offset the dragged item with graphicsLayer { translationY }, not by changing list order each frame. 7. Prevention: Gesture UI test with swipe on the handle asserting scroll offset is unchanged; review rule for consuming in custom detectors; Compose lint for pointerInput(Unit) captures. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not disable list scroll globally (accessibility and flicker); I would not call requestDisallowInterceptTouchEvent (Views concept).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the user drags beyond the viewport? → Autoscroll via LazyListState.scrollBy in a loop driven by drag position.
  • Does Modifier.draggable consume automatically? → Yes, it handles consumption and slop; consider it.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team spent two sprints on custom reorder; the final design used the library state pattern with consumed drags and a keyed list, plus accessibility custom actions "Move up/down".

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: workarounds that disable scrolling.
  • Hire: identifies missing consume and stale capture.
  • Strong hire: also covers autoscroll, keys, translation-based drag visuals and accessibility actions.

questions.promptHtml: How does focus work in Compose? Explain focusRequester, focusable, onFocusChanged ordering, key events, and how to handle keyboard/D-pad navigation.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Forms, TV, Chromebooks and foldables with keyboards all depend on a correct focus model; ordering bugs are subtle.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Focus targets are modifiers (focusable, built into clickable, text fields). Modifier.focusRequester(fr) attaches a handle; I call fr.requestFocus() from an event or LaunchedEffect, never in the composable body. onFocusChanged observes the focus target to its right, so it must sit before focusable. Key events go through onPreviewKeyEvent (parent-first) and onKeyEvent (child-first bubbling). Traversal can be shaped with focusProperties, focusGroup, and focusRestorer.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Modifier order matters: Modifier.onFocusChanged{}.focusRequester(fr).focusable() works; putting onFocusChanged after focusable observes nothing useful. requestFocus() throws if the requester is not attached ("FocusRequester is not initialized": wrong remember, no focusRequester modifier, or called before placement). Initial focus: LaunchedEffect(Unit) { fr.requestFocus() } which runs after composition when the node is attached.

Keyboard: clickable already supports Enter/center D-pad as a click and is focusable; custom onKeyEvent returns true if handled. Preview variant lets a parent intercept (shortcuts) before children (text field). Soft keyboard: IME visibility is controlled via LocalSoftwareKeyboardController and imePadding; text fields request IME on focus. KeyboardActions/ImeAction drive Next/Done with FocusManager.moveFocus(FocusDirection.Down).

Traversal: Tab/arrow keys use geometric search; override with focusProperties { next = other; canFocus = false }; focusGroup() makes a container a single traversal unit; focusRestorer() returns to last focused child.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val fr = remember { FocusRequester() }
var focused by remember { mutableStateOf(false) }
TextField(
    value = v, onValueChange = { v = it },
    modifier = Modifier
        .onFocusChanged { focused = it.isFocused }
        .focusRequester(fr)
)
LaunchedEffect(Unit) { fr.requestFocus() }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• requestFocus() in the composable body (re-runs per recomposition, may crash before attach).
  • onFocusChanged after focusable or text field.
  • Returning true from onKeyEvent too broadly and swallowing text input.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does focus not move in a Dialog? → Dialog is a separate window with its own focus root; request inside it.
  2. How do you dismiss the keyboard on submit? → KeyboardActions(onDone = { keyboard?.hide(); focusManager.clearFocus() }).
  3. Touch mode vs keyboard mode focus highlight? → Focus indication is shown for key navigation; clickable shows focus via indication; taps may clear focus visuals.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: requestFocus. Senior: explains modifier-order observation, traversal customization, key event passes and test strategy with performKeyInput.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A login form's "Next" action did nothing on tablets with keyboards; fix was focusProperties order plus handling Tab consistently.

questions.contextHtml:
A search screen should focus the field and open the keyboard on entry. After a refactor, crash reports: IllegalStateException: FocusRequester is not initialized at ~0.9% of sessions on screen open (low-end devices more), and on a TV build the D-pad cannot reach the clear button. Code:

@Composable
fun SearchBar(query: String, onChange: (String) -> Unit, onClear: () -> Unit) {
    val focusRequester = remember { FocusRequester() }
    if (query.isEmpty()) focusRequester.requestFocus()
    Row {
        TextField(query, onChange, Modifier.focusRequester(focusRequester).onFocusChanged { /* highlight */ })
        Text("Clear", Modifier.padding(8.dp).clickable(onClick = onClear).focusProperties { canFocus = false })
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: Explain both failures and fix them.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Wrap in try/catch" or "delay(100)"; no ordering knowledge.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the crash occur on first composition only? Does the screen sit inside a navigation transition/animation? Is this inside a Dialog/sheet? Why was canFocus=false added (design request?)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Guard the call and ship a hotfix removing the direct call; stop the crash first.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) requestFocus() executed during composition before the node is attached (first composition); (b) repeated calls each recomposition steal focus; (c) transitions delaying attach; (d) wrong focusRequester instance.
  4. How I'd verify: Stack trace points to requestFocus in composition; reproduce on cold start with animation; unit test with createComposeRule; TV: use D-pad key events in test and Layout Inspector semantics focus info.
  5. Root cause: A focus request is side-effecting and needs an attached target; composition is the wrong place. It also re-fires on recomposition whenever query is empty, stealing focus after the user clears the field. On TV the Clear button's canFocus = false was applied after clickable, but also focusProperties configured on a node that is itself the target; D-pad cannot reach it by design.
  6. Fix:
LaunchedEffect(Unit) { focusRequester.requestFocus() }  // once, after attach
TextField(query, onChange, Modifier.focusRequester(focusRequester))
Text("Clear", Modifier.clickable(onClick = onClear).padding(8.dp)) // focusable via clickable

Remove the incorrect canFocus=false, or set focusProperties { right = clearRequester } on the field for explicit traversal. 7. Prevention: Compose UI test asserting assertIsFocused() after launch; code review rule that effects own side effects; TV smoke test with D-pad. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use arbitrary delay (race and flaky); I would not catch the exception.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Focus inside a ModalBottomSheet? → Request from within the sheet content after it is attached.
  • Should the keyboard always appear? → Respect context; use LaunchedEffect plus keyboardController?.show() only if user intent.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite crash cluster lasted 3 releases because it only happened on slow cold starts; the root fix was moving focus side effects into effect handlers across the codebase.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: try/catch or delays.
  • Hire: moves to LaunchedEffect, explains attach timing.
  • Strong hire: explains re-run stealing focus, traversal bug, adds tests including D-pad.

questions.promptHtml: What do Modifier.semantics, clearAndSetSemantics, and mergeDescendants do, and how do they relate to clickable, testing and accessibility?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The semantics tree is what TalkBack and tests see; wrong merging produces unusable screens.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Compose builds a separate semantics tree from semantics modifiers. semantics { } adds properties (role, contentDescription, stateDescription, custom actions) to a node. mergeDescendants = true makes the node a single accessibility unit combining children; clearAndSetSemantics drops children's semantics and replaces them. clickable, toggleable, selectable add click/selection semantics themselves and merge their content, so a row with icon and text reads as one element.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Two trees: merged (default for accessibility and onNodeWith... finders) and unmerged (useUnmergedTree = true). A node with mergeDescendants merges child properties by each property's merge policy (text lists concatenate; onClick keeps first non-null). Modifier.semantics(mergeDescendants = true) is how you make a card focus once in TalkBack. clearAndSetSemantics is for fully custom announcements, e.g., a rating bar announced as "4 out of 5 stars" rather than 5 icons.

Properties that matter: role, stateDescription, contentDescription, heading(), liveRegion, customActions, onClick(label), progressBarRangeInfo, testTag. Component docs note: Button carries role Button so TalkBack says "Button"; a bare clickable does not unless you pass role.

Semantics modifiers are nodes in the chain: order affects which node they attach to relative to layout modifiers (a semantics placed before padding has bounds including padding), which matters for TalkBack focus highlight bounds.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Row(
    Modifier
        .clickable(onClickLabel = "Open chat", role = Role.Button, onClick = open)
        .semantics(mergeDescendants = true) { stateDescription = if (unread) "Unread" else "Read" }
) { Avatar(); Text(name); UnreadDot() }
// custom ratings
Row(Modifier.clearAndSetSemantics { contentDescription = "$stars out of 5 stars" }) { Stars(stars) }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Merging a container that contains separately actionable children (merged away).
  • Setting contentDescription on decorative icons (noise); use null.
  • Using testTag for production logic.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How to test merged vs unmerged? → onNodeWithText(..., useUnmergedTree = true); printToLog("TAG").
  2. Custom swipe action for TalkBack users? → customActions in semantics.
  3. Does semantics affect hit testing? → No; it only informs services/tests.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: contentDescription. Senior: merge policy, unmerged tree debugging, clickable semantics, custom actions for gesture-only features.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An audit found swipe-to-delete rows unusable with TalkBack; custom actions plus merged semantics fixed it.

questions.promptHtml: When would you use Modifier.layout, and what are the performance and correctness implications of graphicsLayer (including alpha and clip) in a modifier chain?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who treat modifiers as styling from those who know they create layout nodes, layers, and offscreen buffers.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Modifier.layout { measurable, constraints -> } lets me change how a single child is measured and placed (custom padding, aspect, baseline offsets) without writing a full Layout; it is single-pass: one measure call on the child. graphicsLayer creates a render-node layer for transformations and effects done on the RenderThread without re-recording children. It is cheap for translate/scale/rotate/alpha=1; but alpha < 1, clip, shadows, blur or CompositingStrategy.Offscreen can force offscreen buffers, which cost memory and fill rate, especially on large areas.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Layout modifiers are processed in chain order: each wraps the next, receives constraints, measures the inner chain and returns a size. Modifier.padding, size, offset are all layout modifiers. Measuring a child twice throws IllegalStateException: a measurable can be measured once per pass.

graphicsLayer {} properties: translationX/Y, scaleX/Y, rotationX/Y/Z, alpha, shape + clip, compositingStrategy, renderEffect, cameraDistance, shadowElevation. Block reads happen in the draw/layer phase. With alpha < 1 and CompositingStrategy.Auto, the layer is rendered offscreen so overlapping children fade as one; ModulateAlpha multiplies each draw call's alpha (no buffer, but overlaps show through). Modifier.clip(shape) is built on graphicsLayer(clip = true), so many clips on many items add layers; prefer background(color, shape) for solid fills and drawBehind when clip is only decorative.

Hit testing and semantics bounds follow layout, not layer transforms in some cases: translation via graphicsLayer moves pointer coordinates correctly in recent versions, but bounds used by accessibility highlight may not; verify behavior for your version and target. Prefer offset {} if accessibility bounds must move.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun Modifier.firstBaselineToTop(top: Dp) = layout { measurable, constraints ->
    val p = measurable.measure(constraints)
    val base = p[FirstBaseline]
    val topPx = top.roundToPx()
    val dy = (topPx - base).coerceAtLeast(0)
    layout(p.width, p.height + dy) { p.placeRelative(0, dy) }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Measuring the child twice.
  • Applying graphicsLayer(alpha = .99f) on a huge container as a "hack".
  • Using many clip(RoundedCornerShape) on scrolling items on low-end GPUs.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. layout vs Layout composable? → layout for one child; Layout for many.
  2. offset vs graphicsLayer translation? → offset changes placement (layout phase, hit bounds), translation is draw-only and cheapest per frame.
  3. How do you find expensive layers? → Perfetto/GPU profiling, overdraw debug, Layout Inspector render info.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: padding then background. Senior: explains the phase of each modifier, single-measure rule, offscreen layer costs and alternatives.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A list with rounded-clipped, semi-transparent cards ran at 45 fps on a low-end GPU until clips became background shapes and alpha moved to the image only.

questions.contextHtml:
A floating video "mini player" can be dragged anywhere. On a 120 Hz device the drag feels laggy; Perfetto shows a janky frame on 22% of drag frames (p95 frame 11.8 ms vs an 8.33 ms budget). Layout Inspector shows the entire PlayerScreen (a heavy composable with the video surface, comments panel and controls) recomposing 120 times per second during drag. Code:

@Composable
fun PlayerScreen(vm: PlayerVm) {
    var offset by remember { mutableStateOf(Offset.Zero) }
    Box(Modifier.fillMaxSize()) {
        CommentsPanel(vm.comments)
        MiniPlayer(
            modifier = Modifier
                .offset(offset.x.dp, offset.y.dp)
                .pointerInput(Unit) { detectDragGestures { _, d -> offset += d } }
        )
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix. Mention unit bugs, phases, and modifier allocation.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use remember for MiniPlayer", "wrap in derivedStateOf", or "lower the frame rate"; misses the unit bug and phase.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the video surface a SurfaceView/TextureView through AndroidView? Does CommentsPanel take unstable params? Release build? Does drag need inertia/fling or snap-to-corner?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Move the offset read into the placement lambda: Modifier.offset { IntOffset(offset.x.roundToInt(), offset.y.roundToInt()) }.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) offset read in composition: each pointer event recomposes PlayerScreen; (b) .dp conversion bug: pixels interpreted as dp so motion is 2.6-3x too fast at 2.6-3x density (drag deltas are px); (c) modifier chain reallocated each recomposition; (d) CommentsPanel not skippable; (e) video surface re-layout.
  4. How I'd verify: Layout Inspector recomposition counts (screen: ~120/s); compose compiler report for CommentsPanel; Perfetto frame timeline; compare with and without lambda form.
  5. Root cause: State read in composition scope invalidates PlayerScreen and everything not skippable under it every touch event. Additionally offset += d is in px but passed as dp.
  6. Fix: Short-term the lambda offset {}; better, graphicsLayer { translationX = offset.x; translationY = offset.y } to be draw-only (pointer input follows). Keep the state close to the draggable and hold it in a State read inside lambdas; use draggable2D per docs when no fling is needed, or detectDragGestures with change.consume(). Long-term: extract the draggable wrapper so only it owns the state, and ensure CommentsPanel is skippable (strong skipping or @Immutable models).
  7. Prevention: Macrobenchmark drag test with FrameTimingMetric; lint for dp conversion of pixel values; add recomposition-count debug overlay.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use animateOffsetAsState for live finger tracking (adds lag); use Animatable.snapTo while dragging then animateTo to snap on release. I would not move the video into compose phase reads of unstable values.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Snap to nearest corner on release? → Use velocity from drag end, Animatable with spring, in a coroutine launched from the gesture scope.
  • Why graphicsLayer over offset? → Skips layout, only updates layer properties; but accessibility/semantic bounds may lag; choose by need.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite mini-player bug combined a px/dp mix-up and a composition-phase read; after the fix recompositions during drag went from per-event to zero.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: remembers things randomly.
  • Hire: identifies phase read and moves to lambda.
  • Strong hire: finds the unit bug, uses graphicsLayer/draggable2D, adds benchmark and snap animation plan.
